The house in committee of supply, Mr. Bury in the chair.
Agriculture - for experiments in fruit products, $10,000.

The last time we were in committee there were two questions asked to which I promised to give answers. The first was in connection with the grant to the Canadian Horticultural Council. That was under the heading of Canadian Horticultural Council under supplementary estimates, 1932-33, vote No. 333, $5,000.
The second question was with reference to the contribution of the United States to the International Agricultural Institute. The contribution passed March 13, 1933, was $48,500.
What are these experiments that are being carried on? We have been experimenting for a long time.

The purpose of these experiments is to see whether some value can be obtained from fruits, in particular apples of a low grade, by making juices to replace some of the common soft drinks now in use like coca cola and so forth. Experiments are being carried on at Middleton and Kentville, Nova Scotia, the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa, and Summerland, British Columbia. This sum of $10,000 has chiefly to do with apparatus, salaries and equipment necessary for this work.

I notice the minister said that experiments were being carried on at Middle-53719- 228J
ton, Nova Scotia. Will he be good enough to explain what the experiments are, how much the government is expending and why it is carrying on experiments at that particular place. Who is getting the benefits of this?

We have a laboratory at the Scotia Gold Products plant at Middleton, the purpose being to test out ciders made from different kinds of apples in various states of ripeness, making special experiments in these juices, following the principle used in the old country of making a cider without the use of pasteurization.
How long has this experiment been going on and how much has it cost the country so far?
Two years, and I believe at Middleton, Nova Scotia, the cost was a little over $2,000 last year.
Why should it take two years and $2,000 to conduct this particular experiment? Surely scientists or whoever are in charge of this should not take two years to find the value of this experiment.

This amount, of course, is mainly to purchase equipment, and some applies on salary. The work is of a very technical nature. We think the results so far are satisfactory. Similar experiments are being and have been carried on in England for quite a number of years. If we succeed in making a satisfactory product from these lower grade apples available in Nova Scotia, as the low grade apples in the culls run around 60 per cent, this will mean a very much enhanced price for this class of fruit to the Nova Scotia fruit farmer and relieve the fresh fruit market of this load of low grade product.

This does not seem to be a
very satisfactory answer. I can understand the department spending three or perhaps six months in an experiment of this kind, but I gather from the minister's statement that they have put scientists or officials of the department into a private enterprise at Middleton, Scotia Gold Products, which manufactures cider and other things. I cannot understand the necessity of having one or more men there for two years. Surely if the men are capable, it should not take two years to find out whether they can do anything with this product. The apple is a very simple product of the farm. It should not be very difficult for these officials to discover whether a particular
Supply-Agriculture-Fruit

grade of cider or something else can be made from this fruit. Is it not a fact that these men are in this factory, and that really, while the government is paying the money, they are doing work for this particular organization?

The only wage we are paying at this plant is that of one scientist. We have the services of the best scientist we could get for this work. The process, as I said before, is complicated, and whether or not the hon. member is disappointed with the results this man has obtained so far, we feel he is the best we can secure for the work.

I am not disappointed; I am not paying this scientist's wages. The government is paying him and the government and the minister should be disappointed. It seems to me there should be no necessity for this scientist to be in this plant for two years. Surely, if he knows his business, as I presume he does, there is no reason for his being in the plant for two years endeavouring to find out whether apples can be made into some liquid. Why is this man there all this time? The government should know now whether he has been able to discover something which will he a benefit either to the government or to the department, and if he is not able to carry out some particular investigation, it is time for the government to bring him back to Ottawa and put him to work on something else.

I do not know of
any question that has been asked.

I asked why the government
is keeping this man at this private plant. It is a private corporation and the government is paying this man's salary. The minister also said that this scientist was sent there to make a certain test as to what could be done with apples. After two years the government should be able to decide whether this man has made the proper investigation and the result of it. I have asked a question

and the minister should be able to answer it-as to what value this man is to the country in the capacity of an official connected with this plant.

One of the results
of his experimental work is a development of fruit concentrates. Last year in this connection there were exported, I believe, 35,000 gallons. The results of these experiments have been made known to all cider plants in the dominion. Many different problems preatr. Duff.]
sent themselves along this line of the study of fruit juices for cider and other beverages. In England, the best men they can get have been working along similar lines for years. We sent Mr. Davis, one of our men, over there three years ago to make a special study. He remained a year in the old country gathering all the information he could and then returned to Canada. We received the benefit of that and he is continuing with this investigation. One of the results has been the development of fruit concentrates. What they are trying to do, as I said at the outset, is to find the best combination of fruit that can be used and under the best conditions it can be used to produce the best product without pasteurization.

The result of having this man at the Middleton plant is that he is making money for a private corporation. If he has been there two years, surely there is no necessity for keeping him there any longer. If I understand correctly he is there looking after the private interests of a private corporation. A minute ago the minister said the man in question made certain juices from fruit. What part of the fruit juice is being exported from the plant as a result of this scientist's investigation?	.

The man is at a
private plant because by having him there we save the government the expense of building a plant to carry on experiments. One result of his work has been that the plant exported 35,000 gallons of fruit concentrate. It is much cheaper to have a man work in a plant already erected than to erect a laboratory for the purpose. The knowledge obtained is not the special property of the plant in which he is working, but is spread throughout the country.

What does the minister mean when he states that 35,000 gallons of concentrates were exported? Are these concentrates just the ordinary cider in bottles that the company sends all over the country?
Mr. RYCKMA.N:	Or is there something
in it?

Yes, or is there something in it? The Minister of National Revenue is interested in that phase of the matter. I may say, for the information of the Minister of National Revenue, that I have heard there is more than two per cent alcoholic content in these concentrates. Perhaps the minister had better investigate.

Supply-Agriculture-Fruit

My information is
that there is no alcohol in the concentrates.

Evidently the Minister of
National Revenue is suspicious. 1 suggest he get in touch with the Minister of Agriculture and have the official send him samples. I am sure the Minister of National Revenue would be able to tell whether the alcoholic content was more than two per cent.
Why would the minister know?

Because he is a good judge.
There is a good deal of complaint in Nova Scotia about the federal government spending all this money, and having an official at a private plant for over two years. I could understand an official being sent to experiment for three months, but surely there is no reason for having him there so long. The minister should give a better explanation than he has given so far why this man is paid a salary for two years, a man who is really an official of a private plant, and doing work for that plant instead of for the government.

He is not doing
work for the private corporation, but for the government, and the entire industry in Canada. Any discoveries made as a result of his research are immediately available to all similar plants throughout Canada.

That does not seem a reasonable explanation. What experiments could he make? What results would it take two years to obtain when only the simple process of making cider from apples is involved? That is all that is being done in the plant. They take apples, grind them up and put them into bottles in cider form. Surely there is no necessity to keep an official at that plant for two years. I want to tell the minister this is nothing more or less than a case of the government keeping an official who, if withdrawn to-morrow, would be replaced by that private corporation. And in that event the private concern would have to pay his salary.
Shall the item carry?
No.

This is an item for $10,000. The minister has told us that $2,000 is used at Middleton for experiments on cider. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough seems to think that the official does nothing but drink cider. Probably that is true, but the other $8,000 must be spent somewhere. We
should like to know at what other points experiments are being carried on, and we want an explanation of the different plants and the work being done in them.

As I said at the outset there is the plant at the central experimental farm in Ottawa and the plants at Kentville and Summerland. In Ottawa, $3,000 is spent, $4,000 at Summerland and the remainder at Kentville.
At Middleton, not Kentville.
Yes, at Kentville.
What work is done at these other places?
Work of a similar nature, but with different fruits. At [DOT] the Summerland station they are carrying on experimental work in connection with dehydrating apricots, prunes and so on.
What are they doing at Kentville?
At Kentville the work is chiefly that of the dehydration of fruits, together with some canning experiments.
What is the work done at the Ottawa experimental station?
Work in connection with fruit juices and canning.
In the event of a discovery made by a man stationed by the government in any of these plants, could a patent be taken out, or is his discovery general knowledge?
The knowledge is general.
Is it at Kentville, Nova Scotia, you have the dehydrating plant, or at Kemptville, just outside of Ottawa?
Kentville, Nova Scotia.
What is the use of having two stations side by side?
They do different work.
What is the difference?

One works on the concentration of juices and the other upon the dehydration of apples, and fruit canning.
Supply-Agriculture-Fruit
Ever since I have been, in the house we have been voting moneys for experiments in the dehydration of fruits. It has occurred to me that the time for experimentation has long since passed.
I think the hon. member knows as well as anybody in the house that there is practically no limit to the carrying on of experiments.
I thought perhaps it had reached a stage where the experiments would have been concluded.

The minister states that there is one scientist at Middleton and another about thirty miles away, at Kentville. The roads between Kentville and Middleton are good. Any man with good, long legs could walk there in a day. Yet we are told there are two scientists doing work for the government, one at Middleton doing certain work and the other at Kentville doing other work. It seems to me one man would be sufficient and I strongly recommend to the minister that he look into the matter. There should not be a man at each point. I would ask the minister to investigate and see that the man at the Middleton station be withdrawn, because I understand the Kentville station is in the nature of an experimental farm. Am I right in that?
It is, yes.

I would not object to having a scientist at Kentville experimental farm. The official at the farm could do any work required by the privately owned bottling works at Middleton. Surely in this time of stress and strain, when we are trying to save all the money we can, there is no need after two years to have a scientist working for a private corporation at Middleton. I strongly recommend that the minister have this man withdrawn from that plant and save that money.
May I ask the minister, would it be possible carry on these two experiments at the one place?

No, the experiments are different. If we did all the work at Kentville it would mean the purchase of laboratory equipment that costs a good deal; it would also mean the use of fruit, bottles and so on that the private plant supplies at Middleton. The scientist at Kentville devotes only part of his time to that, and the rest to fruit breeding.

But the minister must admit
that any investigation which is carried on at the Middleton plant of the private corporation is principally for the benefit of the private corporation.
Not at all.

And if there is a laboratory
there it would be interesting to know who paid for it. If he looked it up I think the minister would find that the government paid. But whether the government or the private corporation paid for it there is no reason why there should be two scientists. The man at Kentville could go to Middleton once or twice a week or oftener if necessary and make any experiments or investigation required. There is no need to have a man situated at the Middleton plant all the time.

How many such investigations as that at Middleton are conducted throughout Canada? I mean, is the information gained at Middleton given to all other plants of a like nature, and how many are there in Canada?

My information is
that there is only this one, and as soon as the information is Obtained it is distributed to all plants for their use.
I was wondering if the old committee that used to have charge of this work is still in existence; I think it was called the dehydrating committee. Is that still in existence?
Yes.
Who are the members?
Dr. Archibald, chairman and Messrs. McIntosh, Macoun, Shutt, Lochhead and MoGillivray in charge of canning.
Are all these experiments made on the recommendation of the committee?
Yes.

None of these
experiments is going on now without their O.K.?
That is my information.

I think it would
be helpful to the committee if the minister would have samples of the cider and these dehydrated fruits. I used to have them in my office out there on the ground floor, and it

Supply-Agriculture-Farms
was quite a popular resort as long as I had the cider and dehydrated fruit. The proof of the pudding is in the eating and I think they would talk much more eloquently than any of us. Joking aside, they are really helpful.

We have stock
samples at the experimental farm here. They are limited, but we shall be glad to show them to anyone who goes out there.

I would like to know
what salary this man a>t Middleton gets, what his qualifications are, and where he worked before he went there. He is said to be a scientist, but he gets less than $2,000 a year; he cannot be much of a scientist.
Do you want to pay him more?

His salary is a
little over 81,700. He received his training in England. He is English born, I believe; he came to Canada, operated a small plant, then went back to England and made further studies and investigations, and came back to undertake this work for us.
What were his qualifications? Is he a B. Sc.?
Did the Civil Service Commission appoint him?

He did take a
science course in England, but I cannot say what degree he obtained. It is a civil service appointment, and they no doubt looked into his qualifications.

When was he appointed by
the Civil Service Commission, and who recommended him to the department and the commission?
An open advertisement, I 'believe, in the regular form, two years ago. I cannot give any information about who recommended him.
He was not connected with the department before two years ago?
No.

Who recommended him to
the department, and why did they get the Civil Service Commission to call for applications?
Because the dehydration committee recommended that the work be undertaken. This was the cheapest way to undertake it, and on their application the Civil Service Commission filled the position.
Who are the dehydration committee?

I named them a
moment ago.

Item agreed to.
Experimental farms, $1,642,000.

Has my hon. friend anything new to relate to the committee in regard to the work on the experimental farms? Are there any more than last year, or any less? Has any special work been undertaken, and have there been any changes?

The number of
farms is the same as it was a year ago. There are very many different projects, some that have been continued for some time, and there are always new problems and projects arising.

What about the
Rosthem farm?

It is still in operation. The work and the staff were curtailed a good deal, because we felt that we were there duplicating work done at the university of Saskatchewan. The work carried on at Rosthem was chiefly in connection with live stock, the dairy herd, pigs and poultry, and some horticulture.

The farm is not
really closed yet?
No.

You are sort of
half on and half off; is that the way?
The same as last year.
I think it is a little different. I believe the superintendent is gone now.
He went last year.

There is a feeling in that community that Mr. Munro, the former superintendent, was let out rather summarily. Has my hon. friend any explanation to make? Mr. Munro was there, I understand, for about twenty-five years, and then suddenly he was dropped like a hot potato. It is rather serious under these conditions to drop a good servant without using every endeavour to place him elsewhere.

It was for no criticism of Mr. Munro's work. It was felt that work was being duplicated at Rosthern experimental farm that was being done at Scott on the one side and at the university on the other, and we felt that with the reduced staff we could

Supply-A gricul ture-Farms
carry on all the work there that was not being done at Scott or at the university. But there is no suggestion of criticism of any kind of Mr. Munro's work, and as soon as opportunity arises, if another farm is opened or a vacancy occurs for which it is felt he would be particularly suited, he will get every preference.
Where is he?
I believe in Prince Albert.

I am very glad to hear what the minister has just said, because Mr. Munro was a very faithful servant, and it is rather like getting the cold shoulder to be dropped as quickly as he was. I might point out that my hon. friend cannot reduce his estimates by $3,000,000 or more and still contend that there is no material reduction in the work carried on. There must be a very material reduction in the work; that is unavoidable. I am not criticizing that at the moment, but you cannot reduce the estimates and continue to give the same service; I know that, and I think the minister knows it also. Of course it is his business to see that the neglect of the work is as little as possible, but I say it cannot be done. I should be very glad to hear of Mr. Munro being appointed, because good superintendents, while they are not as scarce as hen's teeth, are a joy to find, and it is a sad thing to lose one under any circumstances.

I see an increase of $100,000 in this item. For the last few years the matter has been before the department, and on several occasions I have discussed it verbally with the minister of the establishment of an experimental farm for central and northern British Columbia. As the minister knows this was recommended by his predecessor, the hon. member for Melville, and also by Hon. Mr. Tolmie when he was Minister of Agriculture. Last year I understood the minister to say that the department was contemplating closing one experimental farm in British Columbia, I think he said the Windermere farm, and that part of the money saved would be applied to that settled part of British Columbia to which I refer. I know that last summer, when the associated boards of trade held their meeting at which I was present, a resolution was sent to the minister asking for the establishment of such a farm. Since then I -have been asked on several occasions what has been done. I wrote the minister, but he replied that he had no intention of doing anything this year. It seems to me that with an increase of $100,000 
in this item and the closing of the Windermere farm something should be done. I should- like to have the minister explain why no consideration has been given these requests.

There is really no
increase in the item. There has been a change in administration; the revenue known as returnable revenue, which comes from the eggs gathered at egg laying contests and from the sale of some animals and so on, in place of being used by the experimental farms for their own purposes must be turned in to the Receiver General. In addition there has been a ruling that the travelling expenses of the headquarters staff, amounting to $40,000 or $50,000 annually, must be absorbed by each branch. These two items really make up the apparent increase of $100,000, which really is no increase at all.
I might say that we have in contemplation the establishment of a sub-range station in the ranching district of British Columbia, which we think will serve the purpose almost as well as an expensive experimental farm. It will be under the supervision of Mr. Thomson of the Manyberries experimental station, which now has to do with ranching, and I think everyone will agree that he is one of the best authorities we could obtain.

Is that to be
somewhere along the line of the Canadian National?

It will be in the
ranching area. The exact spot has not been decided upon.

I have spoken to the minister on more than- one occasion about a matter which I should like to bring up at this time. In this country there are one or two sections greatly interested in sheep raising, and in my part of the country we have quite a number of farmers intensely interested in that industry. A few years ago they found that nice lambs weighing about 125, 130 or 140 pounds commanded the best price in the market, but last fall when our lambs were ready and the drovers went out to buy, the packers restricted the-m by saying that the minimum weight per lamb should be seventy pounds and the maximum weight one hundred pounds. The drovers in that locality refused to buy lambs unless the maximum was raised to at least 110 pounds. There was a .fixed price for these lambs; those weighing less than 70 pounds were cut to half price, while lambs weighing over 110 pounds were paid for on the basis of half price for everything over that weight. In some instances the packers

Supply-Agriculture-Farms
would not allow anything at all for anything over 110 pounds.
Our people would like to find out where these minimum and maximum weight lambs went. When the ordinary housewife goes to the butcher shops she buys lamb, and it is all the same price. There is no distinction made; she is not told that this cut was taken from a lamb weighing less than 70 pounds while that cut was taken from a lamb weighing more than 110 pounds. She pays the same price for all the lamb she buys. There is a feeling abroad in this country that the Canada Packers and Swift's have a strangle hold on the primary producers; people believe the packers and the stock yards are operating under an overhead that is altogether unfair to the primary producers, and the farmers in Canada would like to know exactly why there should be this discrimination in the price of lamb though there is no distinction made when that lamb is sold in the butcher shops.

I am glad to say that for once I can agree with the hon. member for North Renfrew. There is no question but that this is a serious grievance on the part of the producer. Indeed I was told the other day that a man who had shipped lambs under '-he regulation weight to the Winnipeg market had left only 14 cents per lamb after paying the freight; that is, he received 70 cents for five lambs. There is no doubt that in regard to lambs and hogs under and over weight the producer is heavily discriminated against, and if anything can be done to correct that situation undoubtedly it will be to the benefit of the producer.

I should like to ask the minister if the Manyberries experimental range station comes under this item and, if so, whether he could tell me the cost of conducting that station. I should like to know also if there are other stations in Canada doing similar work.

That is the only station of its kind in Canada, and the cost is approximately 818,000.
Mr. GERSHAW': Then I should like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that a very special work is being done there in connection with the re-grassing of abandoned range land both with regard to winter and summer pasturage; in connection with how cattle gain under certain conditions, and particularly with regard to general range practice. In view of the fact that no other station in Canada is doing
similar work I should like to ask the minister if these reports could be published separately rather than mixed up with the general reports of the department.
They were published separately the last time.

Before leaving the question I brought up I should like to get some assurance from the minister that before the season for marketing lambs comes next fall some action will be taken by the government to see that the primary producer gets fair play. If the position, as I have stated it is not correct, if the farmer is getting all that is legitimately coming to him, I think that that should be known and the reasons for it be made plain to the farmers of this country, but if the packers are taking advantage of the farmers, that also should be made known. If the packers, on the other hand, are acting in good faith and everything is perfectly honest, legitimate and aboveboard, then in order to protect them from a feeling that is prevalent throughout the country, the whole situation should be cleared up. The primary producers would then feel that they were not being treated unfairly and that there was no occasion for any resentment against the packing industries of this country. But I repeat, that there is a feeling throughout Canada and has been for many years amongst the farming community that the packing industries of this country have a stranglehold upon the farmers and have them at their mercy, and many believe that it is about time that that stranglehold was loosened.

I should like, Mr. Chairman, to follow up what my hon. friend has said if it is in order to discuss it on the vote for experimental farms, but personally I think it would properly come under the live stock vote. How do you propose to deal with the matter, Mr. Chairman?

The matter needs to be
fully discussed and I do not see any reason why it should not be discussed on this item as well as on any other.

But if it is discussed under this item it may be discussed all over again under the live stock item.

On a point of order,

Has any additional ground been taken in this year for the experimental farm station at Summerside, Prince Edward Island? Has any additional expenditure been made, or is it in contemplation?
There has been no additional enlargement this year and none is contemplated.

Has any request been
made by the superintendent of the Summer-side station to inorease the number of foxes kept?
I am informed that no such request has been made.
Has no request been made to increase the number of foxes kept, with a view to making the station self-sustaining?

It is quite evident that it would be very difficult, impossible, I think, to put the station on a paying or selfsustaining basis so long as we are endeavouring to carry on the experimental work we are doing.
What was the cost of the operations last year as compared with other years?
In connection with the experimental work that was being carried on at the Summerside station, has some of it been transferred to the experimental plant at Hull, Quebec, or elsewhere?
I think the hon. member has reference to the work that has been carried on at the Hull institute. That is a new kind of work with special reference to the disease of distemper.
That work is being carried on at Hull now?
Yes, it was never done at Summerside.
Who are the men engaged in that work at Hull?
It is under Doctor Watson.
Any assistants?
He is assisted by Dr. Percy J. G. Plummer and Dr. J. R. West.
Is any contact being maintained with the Welcome laboratories in England in connection with this work?
Yes. *
There has been a very insistent demand for an experimental farm somewhere in the Peace River country. Has any headway been made in connection with that proposed project?

As the hon. member knows, there is a substation at Beaver Lodge which is doing very excellent work. I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend that when times are a little more propitious and money is a little more plentiful that work should be extended.

It came to my notice a few weeks ago that the experimental farm has issued circular letters to the farmers in my riding, and I think throughout northern Ontario, asking them what advantages they have found from the demonstration farm, and there is a fear on the part of the farmers that the demonstration farm may be closed. I should like to get the assurance from the minister that no such step will be taken, because such farms as the demonstration farm in the clay belt of northern Ontario at Kapus-kasing, which is one of the best, are of great advantage to the farmers. On account of the long distances it is almost impossible for a good many of the settlers to visit the experimental farm at Ottawa, but they do visit the demonstration farm during the summer months at least. I attended a meeting in northern Ontario at which lectures were given

by agronomists and which was attended by from two hundred to three hundred people at one time. It would be false economy to discontinue these demonstration stations which I believe are being maintained at very little cost to the department and the country as a whole.
There is another matter which I want to bring to the minister's attention. It was understood that two years ago a poultry promoter was to be appointed for northern Ontario and North Timiskaming, and I believe that applications were received for the position. I do not believe that the appointment has yet been made, or at all events no such poultry promoter has ever functioned in northern Ontario. In Quebec they have such a man and he is doing wonderful work. One can readily realize what it means to our settlers, many of whom have graduated to the farming class, and to the industry of agriculture generally when I say that a carload of eggs is brought into the town of Timmins practically every week from outside of our section of the country, whereas under proper direction our own section of the country could supply that demand. We should encourage the settlers and farmers in this section of the country. I am surprised that this official has not been doing anything for the last two years. I understand the appointment has been sanctioned but the position has not been filled. We hear of people being settled in this section of the country and they should be given as much assistance as possible. Could the minister answer the two questions I have answered?

The hon. member's first question was in connection with the illustration stations. I agree with the hon. member that these stations are very important, and there is no intention to curtail their numbers in any way. I am sure he will agree with me when I say that with so many of these stations distributed throughout the country it is necessary that a close check be kept in order to see just what stations are giving value for the money expended. The hon. member's other question would come under the item dealing with live stock, and I shall be glad to look into the matter. I thought there was a possibility it might be a provincial rather than a federal promoter. However, I shall be glad to look into the matter.

The Ontario government closed the demonstration farm at Hearst. There was located at that farm one of the
ablest officials in the country. This gentleman is now working at the Kapuskasing experimental farm. I should like to know if he is in the employ of the federal government.

When the provincial government decided to close the farm at Hearst we made an arrangement whereby the gentleman to whom my hon. friend refers would still continue to carry on extension work for the provincial government with his headquarters at the federal experimental farm at Kapuskasing. He is not an employee of the federal government; he is still with the provincial government but has his headquarters at the farm.

I should like to say a few words in connection with the illustration stations. For the past two or three sessions I have spoken favourably of the work done by these stations. We have two in my constituency one near the town of Kindersley and the other near the village of Lovema. There is a capable man in charge of the Kindersley station and I have always been able to speak very highly of the work accomplished, I do not think I need review at this session the splendid results obtained. I was not able to speak with any authority last year of the work done at Lovema but since last session I have made it my business to get first hand information in connection with that station. I am now able to report to the minister that it is doing splendid work, possibly better than the work done' at Kindersley. This station is in charge of a very competent operator Mr. Robert Brumwell. He has been experimenting with brome, western rye and alfalfa grasses, as well as with different crop rotations. Perhaps the most important work carried on by Mr. Brumwell is in connection with soil drifting. He lives in that section of the province which is subject to considerable soil drifting, and he is carrying on his experiments without any financial assistance from the government. I understand he has a fifty-eight acre plot of ground which he uses for experimental purposes, and, if I am not mistaken, the regular rate paid by the government is $5 per acre. The soil drifting work is something which he is throwing in free of charge. In spite of the very dry weather which has prevailed in the country with accompanying soil drifting, Mr. Brumwell has produced an average of twenty bushels of wheat per acre over a five year period. He has also accomplished considerable in the growing of grasses in soils usually not suitable for this growth. Another important function of this station is the distributing of seed to

Supply-Agricult urc-Farms

the people of the district. Last year Mr. Brumwell had a large quantity of 10-B marquis wheat which he distributed to the settlers. I have a couple of snapshots of this station which I shall send over to the minister. These show the shelter belt and the fruit trees which have been developed as an example to the people of the community. These snaps were taken during the field day held on July 27 of last year, and they give an idea of the interest the people take in that particular station. A few years ago the experimental farm at Scott supplied this supervisor with twenty turkey eggs. From that small beginning he has been able to raise the standard of the turkeys in that district with the result that in 1931 a carload shipped from Loverna weighed two pounds per turkey over the average for the province. The turkeys from the illustration station itself weighed two pounds per turkey higher than the rest of the shipment. The influence of this station upon the turkey business in that district is very remarkable. The field day last July was attended by upwards of 350 persons. According to the reports which appeared in the local paper as well as the report of the man in charge of the illustration station, these people spent a very profitable day inspecting the field plots, viewing the farm exhibit which had been sent down from Scott and listening to addresses dealing with gardening, soil drifting, weed control, the raising of turkeys and such like. Mr. Brumwell concludes his report of the work done by the station by saying:
In my opinion the illustration station is the best method brought forward to date to help solve farm problems and bring reliable first hand information to the farmer.
Those words summarize the lengthy report made by Mr. Brumwell. I hope the minister will continue the illustration stations wherever good work is being done. As far as the two in my own district are concerned, I can speak most highly of what has been accomplished there.
Do I understand that the total cost of all illustration stations in Canada is included in this item of $1,642,000?
Yes.
What is the total cost of operating the illustration stations in the dominion?
$80,000 for 209 stations.
The minister promised to establish a station at Hafford in my constituency; has this matter been settled as yet?

My information is
that it has been.
What is the difference between the work done by an illustration station and that done by an experimental farm?

They are entirely different. The value of the work accomplished by an illustration station depends largely if not entirely upon the work of the experimental farms. The purpose of an illustration station is to illustrate to the people the results which have been obtained at the experimental farms.
For instance in northwestern Saskatchewan or, for that matter, in northern Saskatchewan, we have an experimental farm at Rosthern.
And at Scott.

That is pretty well south; I do not know whether you would include Scott in northern Saskatchewan. But there is a tremendous area northward that is developing very quickly, running from the North Saskatchewan river northward and westward, I understand that two years ago there was quite a demand for another experimental station north of the North Saskatchewan river and the opinion departmentally was voiced that in all likelihood that area would never get an experimental farm. What is the opinion of the minister as to that? That information came from some of the heads of the department.

I am sorry I did
not catch what the hon. member said.

In the part of Saskatchewan known as the northwestern part of the province we have illustration stations, I understand, at Spruce lake-that has not been closed-at Meota, a splendid illustration station under the guidance of Mr. Walter Tait, one of the best farmers in that part of the province; one at Glenbush under Mr. Grant, and another at Meadow Lake. Will there be any opportunity in the future development of that great part of the province, the most productive and coming part of it, for an experimental farm? Must that part of the province always put up with a small number of illustration stations, and is the statement made by departmental officials that the day will never come when there will be an experimental farm in that part of Canada, true?

I do not think any departmental official would be warranted in making such a statement.

I believe the statement
waa made, but if the minister thinks it should not have been, I shall leave the matter at that. If it ever was made, I am here to refute it, I do not care who made it, because the day will come when that part of western Canada should have an experimental farm. It is the park area of northern Saskatchewan and it is quite possible to have there an experimental farm devoted to problems entirely different from those dealt with by a farm established in a differently constituted and differently cultivated area. The question ought to be an open one. I do not think all the evidence is in yet to justify anyone making a ridiculous statement of that kind; but if it actually was made, I shall take the answer of the minister to the effect that it did not mean anything. As I say, the question is an open one and we shall be looking forward at some time in the future to having -as we should-an experimental farm in that part of western Canada.

Some time last year the herd of cattle which the department had at Swift Current was removed to a farm in Alberta. I should like to know from the minister the reason for that removal and whether it is the intention to establish another herd at the Swift Current experimental farm.

Only part of the herd was removed from the Swift Current station. The work thus lost, if one considers it such, has been made up by feeding experiments that are being carried on there this year. Any results of experimental work that are obtained with reference to live stock in any of the experimental farms are, of course, made available to the Swift Current farm and from there, through the illustration stations surrounding it, to the farmers in that area. But we are carrying out there feeding experiments in connection with young lightweight cattle.

I understand the minister has received many protests from people in that area in connection with the removal of that herd. He says that only part of it was removed. My information was that practically the whole herd was removed. I appreciate the fact that the feeding experiments which have been carried on are valuable, but this government and, I believe, the Saskatchewan government as well, for some time have been trying to encourage diversified farming. When that herd was established at the Swift Current station, other experimental stations could get the benefit of the experiments carried on there. I should like to know the reason for removing that herd of cattle. On whose
recommendation was it transferred? After the department has finished the feeding experiments, is it the intention to build up that herd again?

As regards the question of diversified farming, there are more cattle there now under experimentation than there were this time last year. We considered it advisable-and that was the recommendation made to me by my officials-that live stock breeding experiments should be more concentrated.

Did the recommendation for the removal of that herd come from the experimental station in Swift Current or from officials of the department at Ottawa or from officials of the station in Alberta to which the herd was transferred?
No request came from Lacombe. The recommendation came from the department at Ottawa.
Was there any recommendation from the experimental station at Swift Current?
I could not say.
Was the initial recommendation made from the experimental station at Swift Current?

The whole live stock policy on experimental farms is directed by the Dominion Animal Husbandman. He visits the farms in the different provinces, discusses with the men there questions of animal husbandry, returns to Ottaw'a and sits in with the director and other heads of branches. At that meeting the policy for the next year is evolved. In that way it was decided that the change should be made with reference to the herd at Swift Current.

I want to clear this matter up if I can. There has been a reoprt that the officials at the experimental farm at Swift Current were desirous of having those cattle removed. I do not believe that is the fact and I should like to get the minister's assurance to that effect, so that we may have it as a matter of record.
I would say without hesitation that is not the fact.

May I ask the minister what work the Dominion government is doing in the way of experimentation in the control of grasshoppers with respect to both their active control and poisoning?
Supply-Agriculture-Farms

That comes not under the vote under discussion but under the entomology vote passed the last night we were in committee. Continuous studies are being made of the habits of various insects and it is only by such study that means of combating their spread and preventing constant damage can be evolved. There were men in the field practically all last summer, or at least during the period it was necessary for them to be there studying the life habits of those insects. From their observation and the knowledge gained, invaluable information will be given to the provincial authorities who, under the direction to a certain extent of our entomological specialists, will take all steps to avoid the damage which is anticipated this year.

I realize that
the item for the Destructive Insect and Pest Act was passed the other night, but this is really experimental work. Since that vote was passed, I have noticed a dispatch sent out from Ottawa with respect to the grasshopper situation in Manitoba. I have had two or three questions asked me by people in my constituency regarding this matter. The article before me is dated at Ottawa, and I suppose it came from the Department of Agriculture. It is as follows:
Ottawa, Feb. 28.-The prairie provinces are facing invasion. In Manitoba, particularly, will the brunt of battle be felt this summer. The enemy forces in that province alone will number at least 4,356,000,000,000, To combat that force "munition factories" in Manitoba are working day and night and a conference between provincial and federal strategists will be held in Winnipeg, on March 2, when the most intensive plan of campaign ever drawn up in Canada will be decided, it was announced by the Department of Agriculture Monday.
The enemy ? Just the humble but destructive grasshopper. The munitions? Technically they are known as "bait," a combination of "half and half" sawdust, bran and sodium arsenite. The conference? Leading entomologists headed by Norman Criddle.
The war will be waged against a new army but it really is but a continuance of battles which have been carried on for some years against the pest. Last year the invaders claimed 20,000 acres of grain crops but the defenders protected and saved 1,000,000 acres through their preventive measures.
This year Manitoba is preparing for one of its worst invasions in certain areas. It will cost the province in the neighbourhood of $150,000 to wage a battle in an infested area estimated at 1,000,000 acres.
Incidentally the introduction of sawdust in the bait is a Canadian discovery which saved $40,000 last year and which is now accepted in all parts of the continent.
A word about the enemy. One grasshopper lays about 200 eggs at a time, repeating the process four or five times during the season. The eggs are sheltered in "pockets" which confMr. W O. Weir.]
tain from 20 to 65 eggs each and it is estimated that from 100 to 100,000 eggs per square foot will be found over the infested area. It takes a grasshopper about 40 days to mature during which time it changes its coat five times before sprouting wings. Another month or two completes its life span unless it falls prey to the bait. Last year 140 bushels of grasshoppers were killed by this bait to one acre.
To provide the bait, 70 machines are in operation in Manitoba which turn out 100 pounds of bait every five minutes. Some are in operation day and night.
This report comes from Ottawa. I know that the province of Manitoba is expecting to spend $150,000, and local people are working day and night on their machines to save their crops. The question I should like to ask is: How much does the Dominion government pay towards such a campaign?

Nothing, so far as
the material is concerned.

What does the Dominion government really contribute? I think the minister must realize that the grasshopper invasion is really a calamity to the area affected, and my submission is that the dominion should come in and play a greater part than they do at the present time. This year I am afraid it will be far beyond the ability of the province or the municipalities to deal with the area which will be affected.

I think the hon. member will agree, that when he suggests the dominion is not making a contribution he has lost sight of the fact that it is perhaps making the greatest contribution, because were it not for the specialists from the entomological branch who have made such a thorough study in the laboratories and fields and are able beforehand to advise provincial government authorities of the danger, the location of it, when to expect it and its extent, those provincial authorities would be powerless. The policy which has been adopted for some time, and which in my view is a fair one, is that that is our contribution, but that the responsibility of supplying material and the necessary workers to do the actual labour is that of the province and the municipalities.

I appreciate what the minister has said. I know of the very good work that Norman Criddle of Treesbank, Manitoba, is doing, because that gentleman happens to be in my constituency. I know he is cooperating with the provincial Department of Agriculture. Probably the minister can defend his position by saying that the dominion department is attempting to do scientific work. I submit, however, that when

Agriculture-Farms
the people see a statement such as I have read coming from Ottawa they have no appreciation of the Dominion government's share in the matter. I think the minister would be acting for the good of his department were he ito emphasize to a greater extent the very valuable work Mr. Criddle has been doing in the province of Manitoba.
Shall the item carry?

No. There are two more points I should like to clear up before leaving this item. I refer, first, to the intended illustration station at Hafford. The minister said it was practically in the same position as it was a year or so ago. May I ask him what his intentions are in regard to that station? I should like to say the minister very kindly investigated the possibility of an investigation station at Hafford, or had his department do so, and after investigation gave his word that there would be an illustration station at that point. When the minister has given his word to that effect I know it will be kept. I am asking him, however, if he has any further definite information on the point so that the Hafford district will know its position in that connection without delay.

The illustration
station has already been established for this year on the farm of Mr. Hudek.

Before the election of 1930, if I remember correctly, and my memory is fairly good, the previous government investigated the area westward from Meadow Lake towards the Alberta boundary line, and the area of country northwest of North Battle-ford, with a view to establishing an illustration station that would help farmers farm more successfully. There is an illustration station at Spruce Lake and one at Meadow Lake. West of Meadow' Lake and north of Spruce Lake and North Battleford, there is an immense area of country, new productive agricultural land the importance of which, I believe, I called to the attention of the minister since his government took office. I am of the opinion he said he would investigate matters some time in the future. I am not sure whether any investigation has taken place or not, but I should like to know to-night whether the government has any intention of looking into that new area with a view to the establishment of an illustration station there in the near future.
Is Piapot in that district?
No; I think the minister knows the area in question.

I know the district. There is another illustration station somewhere in that northwest area, and I was wondering if that was the one. However, I shall look into the matter and let the hon. member know.

I was not satisfied with the answer I received about the experimental farm in north British Columbia. Are there any experimental plots along the Canadian National railway between Yellowhead pass and Prince Rupert? If so, where are they?
Is the hon. member referring to an experimental farm or an illustration station?
Illustration stations. It would be in the Cariboo and Skeena electoral ridings.

The following
illustration stations are on the main line; McBride, Prince George-there are two in the vicinity of Prince George-Telkwa and Vanderhoof.

I notice in Hansard for 1928 at page 575 Mr. Motherwell who was then Minister of Agriculture made a strong plea that something should be done in that part of the country. Also at page 577 Mr. Tolmie strongly advocated that something be done in that territory, which covers several thousand square miles. I may say that lately they have built at least one country elevator in there, and if given a little encouragement it will be a great country for home builders, which after all is what we are trying to induce people to become. I strongly urge the minister to give the matter his personal consideration. I know he has not been out there himself, but both his predecessors have been there and looked into it and I hope the present minister will do the same.

Some time ago information
was given that a new grass was introduced that gives special promise for certain sections of western Canada, I think it was called crested wheat grass. Can the minister say what progress has been made with that, and if it is fulfilling its promise?

The results obtained from the grass known as crested wheat grass are very satisfactory. Pure line strains have been developed, and every possible means is being employed to propagate them and in-

crease them as quickly as possible. As soon as we have a quantity available it is distributed to three selected or recommended farmers in each of several municipalities on the understanding that they will either pay for it in two payments or else return to the department the same amount of seed, which in turn is distributed. That policy has been carried out on the recommendation of a committee consisting of members of the provincial and federal departments of agriculture. It is being propagated and increased very rapidly.
It is not open for distribution to individual farmers?
Oh, yes.
From the experimental farms?

One farmer in the
southern part of Alberta-I do not recall his name-had a considerable quantity to sell this year, up in the thousands of pounds, of very high class crested wheat grass.

Can the minister give
any information as to the value of this grass in comparison with others?

In nutritive value
I understand that it ranks very high, if not at the top-that is in grasses as distinct from clovers. Not only that, but it is very palatable; horses and cattle prefer it, even when allowed to get quite ripe, to some of the other grasses like western rye grass. It also has the peculiar quality of being able to withstand drought even better than the rye grasses and brome. It becomes dormant during the long drought, and then responds very quickly to the least moisture.

Some of
the experimental farms have been doing considerable work in connection with the testing and demonstration of machinery, how best to handle it, how best to hitch it up, and I think something in connection with the use of tractors. However, the fall in prices has put an end to the tractor business, we are back in the horse-power age. I have often thought that one of the things that disgusts a great many people in working horses is that they do not know how to handle them. Horses require to have their feet trimmed, and some of them geit bad habits, and while there are well known and effective methods of dealing with horses that are what is usually called "mean," the knowledge is not generally distributed. I wonder if it would not be a good thing if some branch of the Department of Agriculture would undertake to collect in a bulletin and distribute to the farmers
[Mr. R. Weir.}
of Canada information as to how to trim horses' feet, how to make them lift their feet, and how to deal with horses that are hard to handle, kickers and so on. I believe it would be of very great help, because some people have literally been driven off the farm on account of their being utterly unable to handle horses.

I believe much information of that nature has been sent out. The hon. member, himself a farmer, will realize that in perhaps the majority of cases, at any rate in a great many, the trouble starts with the man who is handling the horse. However, it is a very good suggestion and we will look into it.

To come back to the
crested wheat grass, Mr. W. H. Moore of Bindloss sold some seed to the department, but his trouble was that he was left with a lot of seed that he could not sell. Can the minister tell me where he might find a market for it?

We shall be glad
to look into that. I might say I helped him out myself to the extent of about one thousand pounds. That is the name I could not think of before. Professor Kirk I know has his name on his list, and I think the last time I spoke to him he thought he would be able to help him dispose of it all. But I shall be glad to refer it to him again.

I would like to ask what

In the neighbourhood of $40,000. The chief work carried on there is in connection with tobacco, and also a great deal of work in connection with soybeans.

At the time the station at Harrow was first established I believe that section of Ontario was perhaps the only part growing tobacco. Since then the Norfolk-Elgin-Oxford district has developed tobacco growing to a much greater extent, and in that section they are now producing almost all the tobacco grown in Ontario. There is a request from the growers of that section and from the board of trade of Delhi that the department establish a station at Delhi for experimental work. in that county. I know that the minister has had a request for the establishment of a station at Delhi, and has had considerable time to think it over. I was wondering if he could tell us now his decision in the matter.

Before this item passes, Mr. Chairman, following your decision that we should discuss marketing at this time I should like to ask the minister whether it is correct that the stockyards throughout Canada are under the control of the federal government and the Department of Agriculture. If that is so, as I think it is, I should like to direct the minister's attention to a condition which I pointed out to him some three or four months ago. Are the fees charged for the use of the stockyards the same in all cases regardless of who brings in the stock and in what manner it is delivered?

I thought the chairman ruled that these questions should be discussed under the live stock vote, which is where I think they should be brought up. However, I may say that we have made a very careful study of the whole stockyard situation during the past year. We feel that there is much that is not to be desired in connection with the way the charges are set out, but according to our information only two stockyards in the dominion are paying dividends. We sent out a letter asking the various stockyards to report as to whether or not they would make a voluntary reduction of ten per cent in certain charges, and in that letter it was intimated that if this was not done a further investigation would have to be carried out. To make it short, however, the point is this: I feel that the charges are too high, but my information does not put me in a position to take the responsibility of saying that they must materially reduce their charges, lest by doing so wo might put some
of them out of business. Until we get further information with regard to their finances I do not feel like taking that responsibility, but with that exception I have no doubt a reduction could be made.

There is one point I should like to draw to the attention of the minister, and no doubt it has been mentioned previously. Let us take for example the stock yards of Saskatoon or Moose Jaw. To-day a farmer delivering a truckload of hogs to either of those stockyards is penalized, while a railway carload of hogs receives a certain consideration. As the minister knows, farmers living even some considerable distance from those two stockyards are trucking their hogs, and I should like to know whether the minister is aware of the fact that the farmer who delivers his hogs by truck is being penalized to the extent of one dollar per head. If the minister is aware of that fact could he say why that is being done?
I must say that I did not know of this practice. Does my hon. friend say that if a farmer delivers a truckload of hogs to the stockyards he is liable to that charge?
Yes. Could the minister give the reason why that is so?
Is that where no service is given?

Is this really a penalty imposed on the farmer; is it to prevent the farmer from delivering his hogs by truck or is it to encourage shipment over the railroads? In my humble opinion, Mr. Chairman, whether a farmer delivers his hogs by driving them ahead of him, as is done in Ireland, or by a truck or by the railway, there should be no discrimination. If this has not been drawn to the attention of the minister I think it should be looked into right away.
I appreciate having this drawn to my question. I cannot possibly see how it could be true that there is this discrimination, but I shall be glad to look into the matter.

I can assure the minister that this practice was in vogue as recently as last summer, at all events. We are shipping hogs by truck from in and around the Luseland district, and the farmers are being penalized to the extent of one dollar per head because of that fact.

Would the minister
advise the committee how the vote for the Kapuskasing experimental farm this year compares with the vote last year?

I am quite free to
criticize the parsimony of this government in that regard because when I sat on the government side I found it necessary to criticize the former government for not devoting a larger amount of money to that farm. We in northern Ontario received no benefit from the wheat bonus scheme because we cannot produce wheat, and the stabilization fund created under this budget in order to aid the exporter of farm products will not help us either. The only compensation we have in our part of the country is the Kapuskasing experimental farm, which formerly sold the settlers pedigreed stock and poultry, as well as the produce of the farm, practically at cost prices. Ever since I have been in this house I have had to criticize the Department of Agriculture for not giving that farm the amount of money it should receive, having regard to the large territory it serves and the great benefit it is to the people there.
The manager of that farm is well known to every settler in northern Ontario; I believe he is a personal friend of the Minister of Labour, and there is no doubt that he is the proper man in the proper place. I know he has always found it difficult to make both ends meet. When the big power plant and the Spruce Falls paper plant were being constructed some settlers resented the fact that the horses from the experimental farm were used in competition with the horses of the settlers, but on making inquiry I found that the management of the farm had to find some employment for those horses in order to balance the yearly budget. I maintain that this is not the way to deal with an institution of that kind. Having in mind the work that is being done in placing a large number of families back on the land in our section of the country; having in mind also the fact that most of our settlers find it impossible to go a long distance in order to obtain pedigreed stock, I believe the government should continue the practice of raising cattle on the Kapuskasing experimental farm. I understand that two years ago those in charge of the work of that farm had to curtail that work through lack of funds, and I plead with the Minister of Agriculture to have it undertaken again. Surely the federal treasury should find it 
possible to look after the requirements of our fine agricultural population in northern Ontario.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, the legislation that has been brought forward in this parliament during the last three years may have proved beneficial to other parts of the country. We do not quarrel with that; we are satisfied that $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 should be given the wheat growers of the west, and we are satisfied that the primary producers of eastern Canada as well as of the prairie provinces should benefit to the extent of millions of dollars under this stabilization scheme. But I could easily prove that that will not be worth anything to us, because we are not on an export basis. Surely the Department of Agriculture could find it possible not only to maintain the present activities of the Kapuskasing experimental farm but to enlarge them considerably. It would be money well spent. Most of our settlers are not yet farmers and they need pedigreed stock to start new herds, but they cannot afford to come down here and bring them back and pay travelling expenses. In the past, and I give the government credit for this, the experimental farm at Kapuskasing has found it possible to sell at cost price poultry, chickens and hogs, and that has been very beneficial to our section of the country, but under this vote that farm will find it absolutely impossible to continue those activities. I hope the minister will take my plea into serious consideration and find it possible to increase the vote on account of the situation with which we are faced in that part of the country.

With reference to the hiring of horses in the lumber camps, that has not been done in the last two years. So far as reducing the herd of cattle is concerned, as the pure bred stock increased in numbers the grade cattle were disposed of. We are in a position so far as live stock is concerned to give the same service as we have given in the past. I am sure that those in charge of the experimental farm will appreciate this commendation of the work they are doing, especially of the distribution of the best blood lines of live stock to the settlers at cost price.

How much was spent
last year by the experimental farm at . Laooimbe, Alberta, and how much is it proposed to spend this year?

Last year $42,500,
and this year approximately the same.

I am glad that the
amount is not going to be reduced. Indeed, I hope the time will come when the expenditure .may be increased. That farm is no longer in my riding and therefore I cannot speak for it as its representative, but it is within twenty miles of my own home and I continue my practice of visiting it two or three times a year and going over the place in a businesslike way to find out how much money is being spent, whether it is being spent to the best advantage, and where money might be saved.
There are two or three lines of work being carried on there which are very beneficial. First I would mention the number of meetings which are addressed by the superintendent and his staff. They are almost as much embarrassed in that respect as members of parlia-53719-229J
ment, although I believe they are even more popular than many members of parliament. It is a great tribute to their work that they should be asked every year to address an increasing number of meetings. When you add to that the fact that their correspondence is equal almost to that of a department of government and is extending over wider and wider areas, I think that may be taken as a fairly good criterion of the value which the people of that district attach to the work that is being done. One particular piece of work is carried on there in cooperation with the elevator companies-I ' do not know whether it is done in other parts of Canada- which to my mind is a very splendid piece of work. Different elevators are cooperating with the farm and taking from each farmer's wheat as it is hauled in a fair-sized sample of the typical wheat that that farmer sells, and asking him whether he intends to sow that again next year. Then these different samples are sown in small plots on the farm- the farmers whose samples are planted are not known to the superintendent by name at all, each farmer being given a number. When the farmer goes to the station in the fall he can see there his own sample growing alongside samples that have been sent in by other farmers, and when the big field day comes, much interest is taken by hundreds of farmers who come to see the results in their plots, and compare them with that of their neighbours. They can see whether they are getting a mixed grade, or whether their grain is dirty or weedy. To my mind that is one of the most useful pieces of work that can be done, and it certainly is resulting in a great many of the farmers discarding their own seed; and getting better seed.
I have always been a very strong supporter of the experimental farms even in times of economic stress, because I realize, as most farmers do, that no matter what the economic conditions may be and no matter what the market price, the basis of a good price, the foundation of success, must commence with good seed grown under proper conditions and *in a proper way. I just wanted to add my tribute of praise to the work which the experimental farms are doing. We on this side usually criticize the government because that is the duty of members on the opposition side, but I have kept very close watch on the work that this particular farm has been doing for a good many years now, both under the present minister and the former minister. I cannot say that the work is improving particularly because it was always good under both ministers, but the work is certainly being

A very promising
rust resistant wheat was developed at the rust laboratory at Winnipeg and I was wondering if any further progress has been made. It would mean a lot to the farmers if a good rust resistant wheat with sufficient quality of grain and straw were discovered. Is this rust laboratory still under the Department of Agriculture, or has it been changed over to the National Research Council? I frequently see items in the press, especially the Winnipeg press, giving interviews with Doctor Tory after he has made a visit to this laboratory, which leads one to believe that this rust research work is under his charge. Has there been any change in the administration of this laboratory?

Excellent progress
has been made in the development of a rust resistant wheat. Six strains have been developed which are not only rust resistant but which have been found to be quite high in yield, and baking quality. These strains are being increased this year under close super-

vision and it is hoped that some will be available for distribution next year. As the hon. member knows, the greatest precaution must be taken with these wheats. Publicity cannot be given to their development, lest people try to get a few odd heads and try to multiply them without knowing just exactly what they are. As far as the supervision and administration of the rust laboratory is concerned, the building was built by the Department of Agriculture and I understand that every official is paid from the vote of the department. I do not know of any contribution received from outside the department.

What is happening in connection with the poultry disease known as puMorum? We do not hear so much about this work these days. This is a very malignant and contagious disease and I should like to know if its spread has been limited to such a point that no further attention need be given to it; or has this work been taken over by the provincial departments of agriculture?

At the conference
in Toronto and at later discussions a definite policy was discussed with the various provinces. They have practically all agreed in principle to cooperate with the federal government in order to carry on this work at the minimum cost.

The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson) has pleaded long and earnestly, as did his predecessor, for an experimental farm along the old Grand Trunk, as it is called, east of Prince Rupert. My predecessor and the minister's predecessor both gave some assurance to the people out there that the next experimental farm would be located in that territory. That may not have been a wise promise to make but in any event the next farm has not materialized. It is something like to-morrow which never comes. In view of the shrinkage in finances, I would make the suggestion that log cottages and barns be erected in this territory which could be used as pioneer buildings for a future experimental farm layout. There is plenty of timber suitable for construction purposes and the minister and his staff could lay out a farm at very small expense. These would be only log buildings but the times through which we are passing make me think that perhaps we will have to go back somewhat to pioneer days. All that would be necessary would be two or three good axemen and some loggers to get out the timber. Not only a house but a barn could be erected to act as an example to the community. I do not insist that the minister make a reply just now, but I leave

this suggestion with him. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael), the hon. member for North Battle-ford (Mr. McIntosh) and others, speak so highly of the work of the illustration stations. What was the maximum number of these stations?
There were 241 at one time.
How many are there now?
There are 209.

That is not getting more fast. I have no doubt that it has been found that some of these stations were not very active. The value of the work performed is dependent largely upon the character and the ambition and resourcefulness of the man in charge, and no doubt certain stations have to be dropped from time to time. The total number of these stations should be kept up however and not to do so is just another illustration of the penny wise and pound foolish policy of the government in cutting the agriculture estimates. As I have said before, this cannot be done without great sacrifice to agriculture. I do not altogether blame the minister because I know what it is to be in a cabinet of sixteen or seventeen. Every minister wants to get his arm into the bag up to his shoulder, and the other sixteen see to it good and plenty that the seventeenth does not get in too far. I urge that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture be spared. A number of instances have been cited to-night where important services have suffered because of this foolish and unwise policy of saving a few pennies and losing many pounds. I draw this matter to the attention of the three or four colleagues of the minister who are present to-night. Now, a word more cheerful than that. Our interest in Reward wheat has not slackened because of the other rust resistant one that is being developed at Winnipeg. Reward wheat has itself a substantial amount of rust resistance. I think I could ask, without fear of causing too much of a rush: Is this strain sufficiently multiplied to let it out to individual farmers?
Next year we hope it will be.

I wish to say one more thing I had in mind with respect to the Lacombe farm, and what I say as to it will apply to others, but I speak with greater knowledge of it. In view of the statement made by the Minister of Finance as to the ten per cent cut to foe made on these estimates when they come to be spent, may I ask the minister to take this farm into special consideration when the question of cutting the vote for experimental farms by ten per cent comes up. There are some-and no doubt the minister knows of them-where expenditures could be cut without impairing the service, but I can give it as my definite opinion, for what it is worth, that to make a cut on this farm, with which I am more familiar, would mean reducing efficiency and service, because I believe the men on it are now giving every dollar of value and every hour of service they can. To make in this case the ten per cent cut threatened would simply mean reducing the efficiency of the service by at least ten per cent, and in these das's when farms should be run better than usual and not worse, we cannot afford any reduction in efficiency.
